pos: n. (William Bedell, 1571–1642, bishop of Kilmore and patron of the Irish Bible)
etymology: Germanic Wilhelm, resolute protector; English Bedell, a beadle, a parish officer.
biblical_def: William Bedell was an East Anglian minister who had served as chaplain at Venice, became provost of Trinity College Dublin in 1627 and bishop of Kilmore two years later, and then did the one thing the Church of Ireland had mostly refused to do: he learned Irish at the age of fifty-eight and required his clergy to preach in it. He set scholars to translate the Old Testament into Irish, saw the work finished, and could not get it printed; it waited until 1685. When the rising of 1641 broke out his own Irish neighbours protected him, and the people of the district carried him to his grave. The dictionary holds him up as the plainest rebuke to an establishment that had preached the gospel for eighty years in a language its hearers did not speak (1Co 14:9).

webster_full: VERNAC'ULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as one's vernacular tongue.
VER'SION, n. A translation; that which is rendered from another language.

scriptures: So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air.

How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?
So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
corruption_summary: He learned Irish at fifty-eight and got the Old Testament translated into it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the comfortable assumption that preaching has been done once it has been performed. For eighty years the established church in Ireland had proclaimed a Protestant gospel in English to a population that spoke Irish, and then concluded from the lack of converts that the people were obstinate. Bedell drew the other conclusion, which was the obvious one, and acted on it alone against most of his colleagues.

The principle to recover is that the word must be understood to be preached, and that this is not a concession to the hearer but the nature of the task. “So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air” (1Co 14:9). Philip's question assumes the same thing: “Understandest thou what thou readest?” (Act 8:30). And the promise attached to the word honestly sent is unconditional: “it shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11).

pos: n. (Nehemiah Donnellan, d. 1609, archbishop of Tuam and translator of the Irish New Testament)
etymology: Hebrew Nechemyah, the LORD comforts; Irish O Domhnallain, anglicized Donnellan.
biblical_def: Nehemiah Donnellan was a native Irish speaker of a learned Connacht family, a fellow of Trinity College Cambridge, and archbishop of Tuam from 1595. His lasting work is the Irish New Testament, begun by others and carried a long way forward by him, completed by Uilliam O Domhnaill and printed in Dublin in 1602. It was the first book of Scripture ever printed in Irish, and it was done in Irish character on a type specially cut for the purpose. Donnellan is the answer to the claim that nothing was attempted. Something was attempted, by Irishmen, early, and the failure to follow it with an Old Testament and a preaching ministry in the same tongue was a failure of will elsewhere (Rom 10:14).

Act 8:31
And he said, How can I, except some man should guide me? And he desired Philip that he would come up and sit with him.
The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it.
corruption_summary: The first Scripture ever printed in Irish, in Irish type, at Dublin in 1602.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a double one. Some accounts of Irish church history assert that no Protestant effort was ever made in the Irish language, which the 1602 New Testament disproves; others treat that single volume as though it settled the matter, which the following century disproves just as plainly, since no Old Testament was printed for eighty-three more years and most clergy never learned the language at all.

The principle to recover is that the chain from sending to hearing to believing has no missing link that God will supply for us. “How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14). The reader needs a guide in his own speech: “How can I, except some man should guide me?” (Act 8:31). And the publishing is corporate work: “great was the company of those that published it” (Psa 68:11).

pos: n. (Ambrose Ussher, c. 1582–1629, Oriental scholar of Trinity College Dublin)
etymology: Greek Ambrosios, immortal, divine; English Ussher, an usher, a doorkeeper.
biblical_def: Ambrose Ussher was the younger brother of James Ussher and by some accounts the better linguist of the two. A fellow of Trinity College Dublin, he worked in Hebrew, Syriac and Arabic, left a partial fresh translation of the Bible into English with his own notes, and compiled lexicographical material that remained in manuscript. He died at about forty-seven with almost nothing printed. The dictionary places him beside his famous brother deliberately. Two men of one household, one of whom became the most learned churchman in the three kingdoms and the other a name in a college catalogue, and the household had given both of them the same thing to work on. Gifts are distributed, and so is the opportunity to use them (1Co 4:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines manuscript as a writing by hand, not printed, and Syriac as the language of Syria.

SYR'IAC, n. The language of Syria, a dialect of the Aramaic.
FEL'LOW, n. A member of a college that shares its revenues; one of the corporation of a college.

corruption_summary: James Ussher's brother, perhaps the better linguist, dead at forty-seven with nothing printed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the comparison that eats a man alive, and it eats him from either end: the brother of a famous man is measured against the fame, and the famous man is credited with gifts that were in fact shared. Ambrose Ussher's translation and notes survive in manuscript. They were real work and they were never published, and that is simply the shape his course took.

The principle to recover is that the servant's account is of faithfulness in what he was given, and that the reward of unseen work is promised. “Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2). The learning itself was a gift and not an achievement: “God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom” (Dan 1:17). And the Father's arrangement covers the unpublished: “thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly” (Mat 6:4).

pos: n. (Luke Challoner, c. 1550–1613, founder and benefactor of Trinity College Dublin)
etymology: Greek Loukas, of Lucania, through Luke; English Challoner, a maker of blankets or coverlets.
biblical_def: Luke Challoner was one of the small group who founded Trinity College Dublin in 1592 and he spent the rest of his life furnishing it, chiefly by buying books. He travelled to England with money raised for the purpose and brought back the beginning of the library, and he took in hand a boy named James Ussher, taught him, directed his reading, and left him his own books and in due course his daughter. Challoner is a type the church needs and rarely celebrates: the man who builds the institution and trains the one student who will use it better than he could. Paul's chain is of four links, and Challoner is the second one, the one that is never the subject of a sentence (2Ti 2:2).

corruption_summary: He bought the books and taught the boy, and the boy was James Ussher.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the narrowing of Christian service to what can be seen in a pulpit. Challoner raised money, crossed the Irish Sea, bought books, catalogued them, and tutored one promising boy; and the most learned Protestant scholar Ireland produced in that century was the result.

The principle to recover is that the transmission of learning is itself ministry, and that its fruit appears later and elsewhere. “the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2). Solomon describes the economy of such work exactly: “Cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days” (Ecc 11:1). And the division of labour is apostolic: “I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase” (1Co 3:6).

pos: n. (Henry Ussher, c. 1550–1613, archbishop of Armagh and founder of Trinity College Dublin)
etymology: Germanic Heimerich, ruler of the house, through Henry; English Ussher, an usher, a doorkeeper.
biblical_def: Henry Ussher was archdeacon of Dublin and then archbishop of Armagh, and he was the man sent to England in 1591 to obtain the charter for a university in Ireland. He got it, and Trinity College Dublin was founded the next year. He was an uncle of James Ussher and part of the same Dublin network of Protestant families that supplied the Irish church with its leadership for a century. The dictionary notes the charter rather than the mitre. Of everything Henry Ussher did, the errand to London is the part still standing, and the men who were trained in the college he chartered include the authors of the Irish Articles of 1615, the most thoroughly Calvinistic confession any established church in these islands ever adopted (Psa 48:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines charter as a written instrument granting rights or privileges, and university as a seminary of the highest kind.
webster_full: CHAR'TER, n. A written instrument, executed with usual forms, given as evidence of a grant, contract, or whatever is done between man and man.
UNIVERS'ITY, n. An assemblage of colleges established in any place, with professors for instructing students in the sciences and other branches of learning.
ARCHDEA'CON, n. An ecclesiastical dignitary next in rank below a bishop.
ARTI'CLE, n. A clause or distinct part of an instrument, discourse, or writing; a particular item in a confession of faith.

corruption_summary: He fetched the charter from London, and the college he chartered produced the Irish Articles.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the measurement of a churchman by his office. Henry Ussher held the highest see in Ireland and the thing that outlived him was an errand: a charter obtained, a college founded, and three generations of ministers trained in it, including the men who drew up the Irish Articles under James Ussher's hand.

The principle to recover is that institutions are a form of instruction to the generation that inherits them. “Mark ye well her bulwarks, consider her palaces; that ye may tell it to the generation following” (Psa 48:13). What is written is written for people not yet born: “This shall be written for the generation to come: and the people which shall be created shall praise the LORD” (Psa 102:18). And the prayer over such work is the psalmist's: “establish thou the work of our hands upon us” (Psa 90:17).

pos: n. (Adam Loftus, c. 1533–1605, archbishop of Dublin and first provost of Trinity College Dublin)
etymology: Hebrew Adam, man, of the earth; English Loftus, from a Yorkshire place-name.
biblical_def: Adam Loftus was a Yorkshireman who came to Ireland as a chaplain in 1560 and rose to be archbishop of Armagh, then of Dublin, Lord Chancellor of Ireland, and the first provost of Trinity College Dublin. He held civil and ecclesiastical power together for four decades, enriched his family, quarrelled with successive lord deputies, and was repeatedly accused of using the church's revenues for his own house. He also pushed the foundation of the college through and became its first head. The dictionary gives the record as it stands, in the Chronicler's manner: a mixed reign, with a real work accomplished and a real charge unanswered, and the two set down side by side rather than averaged (1Co 4:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pluralism as the holding of more than one benefice, and simony as the buying or selling of ecclesiastical preferment.
webster_full: PLU'RALIST, n. A clerk or clergyman who holds more ecclesiastical benefices than one, with cure of souls.
SI'MONY, n. The crime of buying or selling ecclesiastical preferment, or of corruptly presenting to an ecclesiastical benefice.
CHAN'CELLOR, n. A judge; the president of a court of chancery; in Ireland, a chief officer of state.
REV'ENUE, n. The annual rents, profits, interest or issues of any species of property; the income of a church.

corruption_summary: Forty years of church and civil power together, a college founded and a charge unanswered.
corruption_paragraphs: The danger is named plainly, because this is the characteristic clerical corruption of the Irish establishment and not a personal eccentricity. A man holding the archbishopric and the Lord Chancellorship at once has nobody above him in either sphere who is not also beneath him in the other, and the Irish church of that century was full of such accumulations. Peter forbids the motive directly: oversight is not to be exercised for filthy lucre.

The principle to recover is that the steward of a church's goods is accountable and the accounting is not to his family. “Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2). The single standard remains: “it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2). And the office is defined by the mouth, not by the revenue: “For the priest's lips should keep knowledge” (Mal 2:7).

etymology: Greek Christophoros, Christ-bearer; English Hampton, from a common place-name meaning home farm.
biblical_def: Christopher Hampton was an Englishman, a fellow of Trinity College Cambridge, who came to Ireland late, became bishop of Derry and then archbishop of Armagh in 1613, and presided over the Irish church in the years when its Convocation adopted the Irish Articles of 1615. Those Articles, drawn chiefly by James Ussher, are the most consistently Reformed confession ever adopted by an established church in the three kingdoms: explicit on predestination, on the perseverance of the saints, on the papacy as antichrist, and on the Lord's Day. Hampton signed them. Twenty years later the Laudian party in Ireland pushed them aside in favour of the English Articles. The dictionary records what was adopted, and who set it aside (Pro 22:28).

SUPERSE'DE, v.t. To make void or useless by superior power; to set aside; to render unnecessary.

corruption_summary: He signed the Irish Articles of 1615, and the Laudians set them aside twenty years later.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names what happened as a loss and names who caused it. The Irish Articles were not a party document smuggled through a sleepy Convocation; they were adopted by the established church of a kingdom and held for twenty years. Their displacement in 1634, under Wentworth and Bramhall, was a deliberate narrowing of the Irish church's confession to make room for a sacramental and ceremonial party that the Articles had excluded.

The principle to recover is that a confession once received is an inheritance and not a draft. “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set” (Pro 22:28). When the way is in doubt the direction of inquiry is backward: “ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16). And the deposit is held, not revised: “keep that which is committed to thy trust” (1Ti 6:20).

pos: n. (John Bramhall, 1594–1663, bishop of Derry and archbishop of Armagh)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious, through John; English Bramhall, from a Cheshire place-name.
biblical_def: John Bramhall was the ablest of the Laudian party in Ireland and the chief instrument of its policy. Brought over by Lord Deputy Wentworth in 1633, he recovered a great deal of alienated church property, which was a real reform, and used the same energy to impose the English Articles and canons on the Irish church in place of the Irish Articles of 1615, to enforce ceremonial conformity, and to drive the Scots Presbyterian ministers of Ulster out of their parishes. He also wrote a formidable defence of free will against Thomas Hobbes. He went into exile in the civil war and returned as archbishop of Armagh in 1661. The dictionary honours the writing against Hobbes and names the policy as what it was (Act 5:29).

CER'EMONIAL, a. Relating to ceremony or external rite; ritual; according to the forms of established rites.
DEPRIVE', v.t. To divest of an office or dignity; to depose; to take away from.

corruption_summary: He recovered the church's lands and drove the Ulster Presbyterians out of their parishes.
corruption_paragraphs: The error is named precisely and it is not that Bramhall held episcopal government, which was the Church of Ireland's settled order and no scandal in itself. It is that he used the civil power to deprive faithful preaching ministers of their congregations over ceremonies that Scripture nowhere commands, in a country starved of preaching. The regulative principle of worship cuts exactly here: what God has not commanded in his worship may not be imposed, and least of all imposed by a magistrate's warrant on pain of a man's livelihood.

The principle to recover is that obedience to the magistrate is real and bounded by obedience to God. “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). The apostles put the question back to the council rather than answering for it: “Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye” (Act 4:19). The power itself is ordained: “the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1). And the spheres are divided: “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21).

pos: n. (Robert Echlin, 1576–1635, bishop of Down and Connor)
etymology: Germanic Hrodberht, bright in fame, through Robert; Scottish Echlin, from a Fife family name.
biblical_def: Robert Echlin was a Scot, bishop of Down and Connor from 1613, and for nearly twenty years he did something quietly remarkable: he ordained and tolerated in his diocese the Scots Presbyterian ministers of the Ulster plantation, men who would not use the whole English liturgy, because they were preaching and his people needed preaching. Under those men the revival at Six Mile Water broke out in 1625. Then the pressure came from Dublin and from Laud, and in 1631 Echlin silenced four of them, including Robert Blair and John Livingstone. He died four years later. The dictionary gives the record whole, and the whole of it is a case study in the cost of a quiet accommodation made without a principle to defend it (Pro 29:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines connivance as voluntary blindness to an act, and suspension as a temporary removal from office.
webster_full: CONNI'VANCE, n. Voluntary blindness to an act; intentional forbearance to see a fault or other act, generally implying consent.
SUSPEN'SION, n. A temporary removal of a person from the exercise of an office; the act of debarring from a privilege.
TOLERA'TION, n. The allowance of that which is not wholly approved; the allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state.
REVI'VAL, n. Renewed and more active attention to religion; the awakening of men to a sense of their condition.
scriptures: The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.
Joh 4:35
Say not ye, There are yet four months, and then cometh harvest? behold, I say unto you, Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest.
corruption_summary: Twenty years of quiet toleration, a revival under it, and four ministers silenced at the end.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names the weakness without discounting the good done. For twenty years Echlin let the Presbyterian preachers work, and the Six Mile Water awakening and the churches that grew out of it are the fruit of that forbearance. But it was forbearance, not conviction. He had never defended it on principle, so when the pressure came he had nothing to stand on and he silenced the very men whose ministry had filled his churches.

The principle to recover is that a position held only by convenience will not hold under pressure, and the fear of man is the ordinary mechanism. “The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe” (Pro 29:25). The apostles' answer to the same pressure was a settled one: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). And the harvest those men were reaping was real: “He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing” (Psa 126:6).

pos: n. (Henry Leslie, 1580–1661, bishop of Down and Connor)
etymology: Germanic Heimerich, ruler of the house, through Henry; Scottish Leslie, from an Aberdeenshire place-name.
biblical_def: Henry Leslie succeeded Robert Echlin at Down and Connor in 1635 and did without hesitation what Echlin had done reluctantly. He held a public conference with the Presbyterian ministers of his diocese, preached a sermon against them, deposed and excommunicated five of them, and drove a substantial part of the Ulster Scots ministry across the sea; the ships that carried them away and the Black Oath imposed on their people in 1639 belong to the same policy. He was himself driven out in the rebellion of 1641 and died in Wales. The dictionary records the sequence without satisfaction. A bishop who clears his diocese of preachers by the magistrate's arm has not strengthened the church he governs, and within six years he had no diocese at all (Mat 26:52).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines excommunicate as to expel from the communion of the church, and oath as a solemn affirmation with an appeal to God.
webster_full: EXCOMMU'NICATE, v.t. To expel from communion; to eject from the communion of the church and the participation of its ordinances.
OATH, n. A solemn affirmation or declaration, made with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed.
DEPO'SE, v.t. To divest of office; to remove from a throne or other high station.
CON'FERENCE, n. A meeting of two or more persons for consulting on some serious matter; a formal discussion.
scriptures: Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
Act 4:19
But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye.
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
corruption_summary: He cleared his diocese of Presbyterian preachers, and six years later had no diocese.
corruption_paragraphs: The error is named directly: the use of civil coercion to settle a question of worship among men who confessed the same gospel. Leslie and the Ulster Presbyterians agreed on the Trinity, the atonement, justification by faith and the authority of Scripture, and they differed on government and ceremony. He excommunicated them over the difference and used the state to enforce it, and the Black Oath of 1639, which required the Ulster Scots to abjure resistance under penalty, is the policy's logical end.

The principle to recover is that the shepherd's authority is for feeding and not for clearing, and that coercion recoils. “Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52). The council's claim was answered with a question: “Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye” (Act 4:19). And the charge given to overseers is a single verb: “to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28).
